import: Loads a library so its functions can be used in this file.
as: Gives the imported library a short nickname. 'import numpy as np' lets you write np.array instead of numpy.array.
np: The conventional nickname for the NumPy library. Everything after 'np.' comes from NumPy.
pd: The conventional nickname for the Pandas library. Everything after 'pd.' comes from Pandas.
print: Shows a value in the Output panel.
for: Repeats the indented lines once for each item in a collection.
in: With 'for', names the collection being looped over. On its own, tests membership: 'Sara' in credits.
def: Starts the definition of a function.
return: Ends the function and hands this value back to the caller.
lambda: A small one-line function without a name. 'lambda g: g.mean()' takes g and returns g.mean().
try: Runs the indented lines; if one of them raises an error, Python jumps to the matching 'except' instead of stopping.
except: The lines that run when the 'try' block above raises the named error.
.array: Builds a NumPy array from a list. A list of lists gives a 2-D array (a table).
.arange: Like Python's range, but returns a NumPy array: np.arange(3) is [0 1 2].
.ones: Makes an array of the given shape filled with 1.0.
.zeros: Makes an array of the given shape filled with 0.0.
.newaxis: Inserts a new dimension of length 1. a[:, np.newaxis] turns shape (3,) into a column of shape (3, 1).
.shape: The size of the array along each dimension, as a tuple. (3, 4) means 3 rows and 4 columns; (3,) means one dimension with 3 values.
.reshape: Returns the same values arranged in a new shape. The total number of values must stay the same.
.broadcast_shapes: Applies the broadcasting rules to shapes only and returns the result shape, or raises ValueError if the shapes are incompatible.
axis: The dimension an operation runs along. axis=0 works down the rows and gives one result per column; axis=1 works across the columns and gives one result per row.
keepdims: keepdims=True keeps the collapsed dimension with length 1, so shape (3, 4) becomes (3, 1) instead of (3,). That makes the result broadcast back against the original.
.sum: Adds the values up. With axis=0 or axis=1 it adds along that dimension only.
.mean: The average. On an array, use axis to average along one dimension; on a GroupBy, it gives one average per group.
.std: The standard deviation: how spread out the values are around the mean.
.max: The largest value (per column, row or group, depending on what it is called on).
.min: The smallest value (per column, row or group, depending on what it is called on).
.round: Rounds to the given number of decimal places.
.DataFrame: Builds a table from a dictionary: each key becomes a column name and each list becomes that column's values.
.groupby: Splits the table into groups that share the same value in the given column. Nothing is computed until you ask for a result such as .mean().
.agg: Short for aggregate: reduces each group to summary values. Accepts a function name such as 'mean', a list of names, or named results written as new_name=(column, function).
.transform: On a GroupBy: computes a value per group, then repeats it for every row of that group. The result has as many rows as the original table.
.filter: On a GroupBy: keeps or drops whole groups. The function receives one group and must return True (keep) or False (drop).
.apply: On a GroupBy: runs any function on each group and stitches the results together. The most flexible option, and the slowest.
.size: The total number of elements in an array. On a GroupBy, .size() gives the number of rows in each group.
.count: The number of non-missing values (per column or per group).
.unique: The distinct values in a column, in order of first appearance.
.reset_index: Moves the index (for example the group labels) back into an ordinary column and numbers the rows 0, 1, 2, …
.sort_values: Sorts the rows by the values in the given column.
and: Combines two single True/False values. It does NOT work on arrays or columns: use & there.
or: True if either single value is true. It does NOT work on arrays or columns: use | there.
len: The number of items: elements of a list, rows of a table.
range: The whole numbers from 0 up to (not including) the given number.
type: Tells you what kind of object a value is.
time: Python's standard timing module. time.perf_counter() reads a precise clock.
.perf_counter: Reads a precise clock, in seconds. Subtract two readings to time a piece of code.
.dtype: The type shared by every element of an array, or by every value in a column.
.dtypes: The type of each column of a table.
.ndim: The number of dimensions: 1 for a row of values, 2 for a table.
.full: Makes an array of the given shape filled with one value you choose.
.linspace: Evenly spaced numbers between two ends, both included. You choose how many.
.eye: The identity matrix: 1 on the diagonal, 0 elsewhere.
.empty: Makes an array of the given shape without setting its values. Fast, but the contents are meaningless until you fill them.
.copy: Makes an independent copy, so changing it cannot change the original.
.concatenate: Joins arrays end to end along an existing dimension.
.vstack: Stacks arrays on top of each other, as rows.
.split: On an array: cuts it at the given positions. On text (.str.split): cuts each value into pieces at spaces or at the given separator.
.allclose: True if two arrays are equal within a tiny rounding tolerance. Use it instead of == for decimals.
.abs: The absolute value: drops the minus sign.
.sqrt: The square root of every element.
.exp: e raised to the power of every element.
.reduce: Applies an operation repeatedly until one value is left. np.add.reduce(x) is the sum.
.accumulate: Like reduce, but keeps every intermediate result: a running total.
.outer: Applies an operation to every pair of elements from two arrays, giving a table.
.argmax: The position of the largest value.
.argmin: The position of the smallest value.
.nan: NumPy's marker for a missing number. Any arithmetic with it gives nan again.
.nanmax: The largest value, ignoring missing values.
.any: True if at least one element is True.
.all: True only if every element is True.
.sort: np.sort(x) returns a sorted copy. x.sort() sorts x itself and returns None.
.argsort: The positions that would put the array in order, smallest first. Use them to reorder another array the same way.
.partition: Puts the k smallest values first without fully sorting. Faster than a sort when you only need the smallest few.
.default_rng: Creates a random number generator. Giving it a seed makes the results repeatable.
.integers: Random whole numbers from the first value up to, but not including, the second.
.random: Random decimals from 0 up to, but not including, 1.
.normal: Random numbers from a bell curve with the given centre and spread.
.choice: Picks at random from the given items.
.shuffle: Rearranges the array in random order, in place.
.T: The transpose: rows become columns and columns become rows.
.det: The determinant of a square matrix. Zero means the matrix has no inverse.
.inv: The inverse of a square matrix.
.solve: Solves the system of equations A x = b for x.
.tolist: Converts to an ordinary Python list.
.Series: Builds a labelled column from a list (plus an optional index) or from a dictionary, whose keys become the labels.
.values: The data without the labels, as a NumPy array.
.read_csv: Reads a comma-separated text file into a DataFrame. The first line gives the column names.
.read_json: Reads a JSON file into a DataFrame.
.head: The first rows of a table: five unless you give another number.
.isna: True where a value is missing, False elsewhere.
.notna: True where a value is present, False where it is missing.
.loc: Selects by LABEL: df.loc[rows, columns]. A label slice includes its end.
.iloc: Selects by POSITION, counting from 0: df.iloc[rows, columns]. A slice excludes its end, as in plain Python.
.isin: True where the value is one of those in the given list.
.add: Addition as a function or method. In Pandas, a.add(b, fill_value=0) uses 0 where one side has no entry, instead of giving NaN.
fill_value: The value to use where one side has no entry, instead of producing NaN.
.dropna: Removes rows that contain missing values (or columns, with axis=1). subset= limits the check to the named columns.
subset: Limits the check to the named columns.
.fillna: Replaces missing values with the value you give.
.ffill: Forward fill: replaces each missing value with the last known value before it.
.bfill: Backward fill: replaces each missing value with the next known value after it.
.to_numeric: Converts text to numbers. With errors='coerce', anything that cannot be converted becomes NaN instead of stopping with an error.
errors: What to do with values that cannot be converted. 'coerce' turns them into NaN.
.value_counts: Counts how many times each distinct value occurs, most frequent first.
.median: The middle value when the values are sorted. Less affected by extreme values than the mean.
.str: Gives access to text methods that run on every value of the column at once, skipping missing values.
.strip: Removes spaces from both ends of the text.
.title: Capital first letter of each word, the rest lower case.
.lower: Converts the text to lower case.
.contains: True where the text contains the given piece.
.set_index: Uses one or more columns as the row labels. Two columns give a two-level (hierarchical) index.
.unstack: Moves the inner level of the row labels up into the columns: long becomes wide.
.stack: Moves the column labels down into the row labels: wide becomes long.
.astype: Converts to another type, for example .astype(str) or .astype(float).
.concat: Glues tables together: one under the other by default, or side by side with axis=1.
ignore_index: ignore_index=True throws away the old row labels and numbers the rows 0, 1, 2, …
join: In concat: 'outer' keeps every column (the default), 'inner' keeps only the columns all tables share.
.merge: Joins two tables on a key column, putting together the rows that have the same key value.
on: The name of the key column, when it has the same name in both tables.
left_on: The key column's name in the left (first) table.
right_on: The key column's name in the right (second) table.
how: Which rows to keep: 'inner' (keys in both), 'left', 'right', or 'outer' (everything).
.describe: A quick statistical summary: count, mean, spread, minimum, quartiles and maximum.
.drop_duplicates: Removes rows that are exact repeats of an earlier row.
.duplicated: True for each row that is an exact repeat of an earlier row.
ascending: ascending=False sorts from largest to smallest.
.pivot_table: Builds a grid: one column's values become the rows (index=), another's become the columns (columns=), and each cell summarises the matching rows (aggfunc=).
aggfunc: The summary used for each cell or group, such as 'sum', 'mean' or 'count'. In pivot_table the default is the mean.
margins: margins=True adds a row and a column of overall totals.
.to_datetime: Converts text such as '2025-03-01' into real dates that can be compared, sorted and taken apart.
.dt: Gives access to the parts of a date column: .dt.year, .dt.month, .dt.day_name() and more.
.day_name: The name of the weekday, such as Monday.
.resample: A groupby for time: groups rows into regular periods. 'ME' is month end, 'W' is week, 'D' is day.
.rolling: A moving window of the given length. .rolling(7).mean() is a 7-row moving average.
.shift: Moves the values down by the given number of rows, so each row can be compared with an earlier one.
.idxmax: The LABEL of the largest value (for an array position, use argmax).
.query: Filters rows using a condition written as text, with column names used directly.
.corr: The correlation between every pair of numeric columns, from -1 to 1.
.items: Pairs of (key, value) from a dictionary.
